title: Alakshmi Out, Lakshmi In
hookLine: a stove scrubbed at 10pm before Diwali, and a hymn that gives misfortune a face and shows it the door
tomorrow: is Lakshmi only the goddess of money?
last: THE BILVA, BORN OF HER TAPAS.

cards: A home can have a corner that sags. The junk drawer that won't close. The sink that's been full since Tuesday.
The pile of mail nobody wants to open. None of it is a disaster. But walk into a room like that when you're already tired, and something heavy can settle on the shoulders.
The Sri Sukta has a name for that heaviness, and it isn't shy about it. A few lines ago the singer asked for misfortune to be gone. Today the hymn describes her, and then rolls up its sleeves.

teach.b: Hunger and thirst and grime, the elder one, Alakshmi: I drive her away. Non-prosperity, lack, all of it, push it out of my house. Alakshmi is the hymn's word for misfortune, the shadow of Lakshmi.
And look at what she's made of. Not curses or monsters. Hunger.
Thirst. Dirt. The ordinary signs of a house that's struggling.

Then the word elder. In later tellings, tradition makes Alakshmi Lakshmi's older sister, and some honor her as a goddess in her own right, as Jyeshtha, the elder. The hymn itself just gives the word and moves on.
Now the grammar, because it's the surprise. The first verb is I.

teach.h: I DRIVE HER AWAY; YOU FINISH IT.
teach.b: I drive her away. For once, the singer isn't only asking; he takes part. Then he turns back to the goddess: you, push the rest out of my house.
Many teachers read a partnership in that: the person sweeps, and grace finishes the work.
And here is a big reason Hindu families clean so hard before Diwali. Scrubbing, whitewashing, throwing out what's broken.
Many say it plainly: Alakshmi out, Lakshmi in. In parts of Bengal, families even see a small figure of Alakshmi out of the house before Lakshmi is worshipped.
Fortune in this hymn lives in a household, and a household has dishes and floors and a pantry to keep. Misfortune here isn't a fate from the sky.
It has a face and an address, and the family is willing to show it the door, before the lamps are lit and the guest comes in.

how: Some Hindu households clean the house thoroughly before Diwali and Lakshmi worship, and some describe it as clearing Alakshmi out before welcoming Lakshmi in.

o: a spell to curse a rival's house with bad luck
a cleaning ritual done only on New Year's Day
a hymn where the singer helps drive misfortune out

games.q: the one shown the door — tap the pairs.

s: in the hymn, misfortune is a monster from the sky
she's made of hunger, thirst and grime: the signs of a struggling house.
the singer says I drive her away
for once he takes part, then asks the goddess to push the rest out.
the hymn tells the full story of Lakshmi's elder sister
it just calls her the elder one; the sister story comes from later tradition.

games.q: you're the singer, and misfortune is in your house: hunger, thirst, grime. what do you say?
o: goddess, you do all of it.
I drive her away; you push the rest out of my house.
games.why: the line begins with the singer's own verb, I drive her away, then turns to the goddess to push all lack out of the house.

practice: In your mind, find the corner of your home that sags, the drawer, the sink, the pile, and look at it honestly, without scolding yourself.
Then picture it clear, one surface empty and wiped, and breathe there; after this, clear it for real, the way families do before Diwali.
If you pray, you can ask the goddess, or God, for help with the part you can't do alone; if you don't, simply decide which small part is yours.

wordCard.voice: The Sri Sukta. A hymn that names Alakshmi, the elder one, made of hunger, thirst and grime, and says: I drive her away; you push the rest out of my house.

orig.note: Sanskrit: alakṣmīm, misfortune, named in the Sri Sukta as the elder one to be driven out.

carryVoice: Your line: Alakshmi out, Lakshmi in. You do your part, and grace finishes the work. Rest well.

sources.ref: Sri Sukta, verses 7–8 (Rig Veda khila, as commonly recited)
